title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the turbine rotor shaft's primary mechanical function.
student: What is the primary mechanical function of the turbine rotor shaft?
instructor: The rotor shaft supports the turbine stages and transmits torque and mechanical power generated by the fluid-driven blades to the connected drivetrain or generator.

title: Source of Torsional Loading
learningObjectives: Explain how turbine stages create shaft torsion.
student: How do the turbine blade stages create torsional loading in the rotor shaft?
instructor: Fluid forces acting on the blades create moments about the rotor axis. These moments are transferred through the blade roots and rotor disks into the shaft as torque.

title: Supports and Restraints
learningObjectives: Describe the journal bearings' physical role.
student: What is the mechanical role of the rotor bearings, and what motion do they permit?
instructor: The journal bearings support and align the shaft radially while permitting rotation about the shaft axis. In the torsion-only model they do not resist torque about that axis.

title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque transfer through the turbine rotor.
student: Trace the torsional load path from the working fluid to the drivetrain.
instructor: Working-fluid forces act on the blades; the blade rows transfer torque into the rotor disks; the disks transfer torque into the shaft; and the shaft carries the accumulated torque toward the restrained or connected drivetrain location.

title: Relevant Mechanical Responses
learningObjectives: Identify the principal shaft responses in torsion.
student: What shaft responses are important when evaluating the torsional behavior of the rotor?
instructor: The central responses are torsional shear stress for strength and angular twist for torsional stiffness and relative rotational alignment.

title: Effect of Distributed Loading
learningObjectives: Explain why internal torque varies through the active stage region.
student: Why can the torque carried by the shaft vary along the turbine-stage region rather than remain constant?
instructor: Torque is introduced over many axial locations by successive blade stages. As torque is accumulated along the rotor, the internal torque changes continuously through the loaded region.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify geometric, material, and loading parameters controlling stress and twist.
student: What geometric, material, and loading characteristics would influence shaft stress and twist?
instructor: Relevant characteristics include shaft diameter, length of the torque-producing region, magnitude and spatial distribution of the applied torque, and the shaft material shear modulus.
gradingNotes: At this stage, students should identify physical dependencies without relying on analytical point labels or equations.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the turbine rotor into a distributed-torque shaft model.
student: Convert the real turbine rotor into a simplified one-dimensional Mechanics of Materials model. Show the rotor shaft, journal-bearing support locations, the region over which turbine stages apply torque, the restrained torsional reference location, and a coordinate along the loaded region. Represent the blade-stage loading as a distributed torque rather than as individual blades.
instructor: A suitable model is a prismatic circular shaft supported radially by ideal journal bearings, with one torsionally restrained reference section and an equivalent distributed torque applied over the turbine-stage region. The applied distributed torque intensity must be distinguished from the internal torque resultant.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt their own model before viewing the instructor reference idealization.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the simplified rotor model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the turbine rotor into the simplified torsion model.
instructor: Assume a uniform solid circular shaft; homogeneous isotropic linear-elastic material; Saint-Venant torsion; small twist; constant diameter and shear modulus; ideal journal bearings that carry radial loads but no shaft-axis torque; one section perfectly restrained in rotation; blade size neglected; and distributed torque acting only over the modeled turbine-stage region. Bending, dynamics, thermal gradients, stress concentrations, and fatigue are excluded.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the distributed-torque stress and deformation analysis.
student: Before calculating, describe the sequence required to determine stress and twist from the distributed turbine-stage loading.
instructor: Define the distributed torque intensity; integrate it to obtain the total applied torque and restraining reaction; derive the internal torque function from equilibrium of a cut section; construct the internal torque diagram; compute the shaft polar moment of inertia; integrate internal torque divided by JG to obtain twist; evaluate maximum shear stress; then interpret the governing section and parameter sensitivity.

title: Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: State the torsional boundary conditions in the instructor model.
student: Using the instructor reference model, state the torsional boundary conditions at the journal bearings and at the restrained section.
instructor: The journal bearings support the shaft radially but permit rotation and provide no reaction torque about the shaft axis. Section C is fixed against rotation, so θ(C) = 0 and a torsional reaction develops at C.

title: Distributed Torque Intensity
learningObjectives: Write the linearly varying distributed torque intensity.
student: Write the distributed torque intensity acting over the turbine-stage region.
instructor: With x measured from C toward D, the linearly varying distributed torque intensity is w(x) = wmaxx/L, for 0 ≤ x ≤ L.
gradingNotes: The quantity w(x) has torque-per-length units; it is not an internal torque resultant.

title: Total Applied Torque and Reaction at C
learningObjectives: Calculate the distributed-load resultant and balancing reaction.
student: Determine the total torque applied by the distributed loading and the corresponding reaction torque at the restrained section.
instructor: The total applied torque is the area under the triangular distribution: Ttotal = ∫0Lw(x)dx = wmaxL/2 = {{turbine_total_torque_lbft}} lb·ft. The reaction at C therefore has magnitude {{turbine_reaction_lbft}} lb·ft and acts opposite the distributed turbine-stage torque.

title: Internal Torque Function and Diagram
learningObjectives: Derive and interpret the internal torque function.
student: Derive the internal torque T(x) in the loaded region and identify the shape and endpoint values of its diagram.
instructor: Equilibrium of the portion from x to D gives T(x) = ∫xLw(ξ)dξ = (wmax/(2L))(L2 - x2). The diagram is parabolic: T(0) = wmaxL/2 at C and T(L) = 0 at D. The maximum internal torque therefore occurs at C.

title: Polar Moment of Inertia
learningObjectives: Calculate the shaft polar moment of inertia.
student: Determine the polar moment of inertia of the solid circular shaft.

title: Maximum Torsional Shear Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate the maximum torsional shear stress and locate it.
student: Determine the absolute maximum torsional shear stress and its location.
instructor: The maximum internal torque is {{turbine_total_torque_lbft}} lb·ft = {{turbine_total_torque_lbin}} lb·in at C. Therefore, τmax = Tmax(d/2)/J = {{turbine_tau_psi}} psi = {{turbine_tau_ksi}} ksi. The critical location is the outer surface of the shaft at section C.

title: Angle of Twist from C to D
learningObjectives: Integrate a parabolic internal torque to determine relative twist.
student: Determine the rotation of section D relative to the fixed section C.

title: Torsional Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Compare design changes that reduce shaft stress and twist.
student: Which changes most effectively reduce the shaft stress and twist?
instructor: Increasing shaft diameter is especially effective: maximum stress scales approximately as 1/d3 and twist as 1/d4. Increasing shear modulus G reduces twist but does not reduce elastic stress for a prescribed torque distribution. Reducing the loaded-region length reduces both accumulated torque and twist for a fixed distributed-torque intensity.
gradingNotes: Students should distinguish between changing the total applied torque and changing shaft stiffness.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Summarize the rotor response and provide a bounded recommendation.
student: Use the mechanics results to summarize the torsional response of the rotor and state one appropriate design recommendation or limitation.
gradingNotes: The recommendation must remain a limited static-torsion assessment and identify important omitted behavior.
